heroLead: Mio doesn't get the attention Gaylord or Kalkaska do, but Oscoda County sits on the eastern edge of the Antrim core, and the mineral interests out here deserve the same honest look, not an afterthought offer.
intro: Oscoda County, county seat Mio, sits on the eastern side of the Antrim Shale trend, bordered by the Au Sable State Forest and cut through by the Au Sable River. It's one of the least populated counties in the Lower Peninsula, but the Antrim boom of the late 1980s and 1990s reached out here too, and there's real production history tied to sections across the county, alongside plenty of leased-but-never-drilled acreage from the same era.

We evaluate mineral and royalty interests throughout Oscoda County, from Mio out through the surrounding townships and the land bordering the state forest. Ownership here is heavily tied to old family and timber-era land, much of it now recreational or forest property, with mineral rights that were commonly split off from the surface decades before the current owner ever took title.

sections.heading: Where Oscoda County sits in the Antrim story
paragraphs: The Antrim Shale core is usually described as Otsego, Antrim, Kalkaska, and Montmorency counties, with Oscoda County sitting just to the southeast, a mix of genuine core-adjacent production and flank acreage depending on the specific section. Wells that were drilled here during the boom years behave the same way core wells do, a long, slow, flat decline once dewatering established production, but the density of drilling is generally lighter than in the counties immediately to the north.

That means we treat every Oscoda County interest individually. Some sections have decades of solid production history behind them. Others were leased during the boom and never drilled, which is a completely different situation for a mineral owner.

sections.heading: State forest, timber history, and split mineral ownership
paragraphs: A huge share of Oscoda County is state forest land today, and the private land that remains is heavily driven by the same logging-era history that shaped most of northern Michigan, large tracts sold cheap after the original timber was cut, then subdivided and resold over decades. Mineral rights on a lot of that ground were reserved or sold separately from the surface somewhere in that process.

If you own hunting or forest property in Oscoda County and have never received a royalty check, that doesn't necessarily mean there's no oil and gas activity nearby, it may mean a previous owner kept or sold the minerals separately from what you bought. The Oscoda County register of deeds in Mio holds the recorded chain of title if you want to check.

sections.heading: The honest math on a mature Oscoda County royalty
paragraphs: Where Antrim wells were drilled in this county during the 1990s boom, they're now decades into their production life, and like everywhere else in the play, that means small, steady volumes rather than the bigger numbers those wells made in their early years. If your royalty check has shrunk over the years, that's the expected shape of a mature biogenic shale gas well, not a sign of a problem.

We price interests here off actual current production and your real statements, along with net mineral acres and remaining reserve life, not off a peak-year number from decades ago or a flat county-wide guess.

sections.heading: What we need to evaluate your interest
paragraphs: Bring us your deed or probate paperwork, any royalty statements or division orders you've received, and the legal description if you have it. If you're not sure whether your Oscoda County land was ever leased or drilled, we can help check that too. Given how much of this county's ownership traces through timber-era transactions, it's common for owners to come to us without a full picture, and that's a fine place to start.

faqs.question: Was Oscoda County part of the Antrim Shale drilling boom?
faqs.answer: Parts of it were, particularly sections closer to the core counties to the north, but drilling density here is generally lighter than in Otsego or Antrim County. We check activity specific to your section before saying anything definite.

faqs.question: I own forest land in Oscoda County but never get a royalty check. Why?
faqs.answer: Either there's no production tied to your specific parcel, or the mineral rights were split off and sold or reserved by a previous owner before you took title to the surface. Checking the chain of title at the county register of deeds in Mio will tell you which situation applies.

faqs.question: Why would an old lease from the 1990s on my Oscoda County land no longer be active?
faqs.answer: Leases from that era typically had a primary term of a few years and expired without renewal unless a well was drilled and put into production. If no well went in on your specific tract, the lease has very likely lapsed, leaving your minerals unencumbered.

faqs.question: How does a mature Antrim well's decline affect what my interest is worth?
faqs.answer: A well decades into a long, flat decline produces a fraction of its early volumes, which means smaller royalty checks and a more modest valuation than what the same interest might have commanded during the 1990s boom. We price off current numbers, not old peak years.

faqs.question: What's the first step if I want to sell mineral rights in Oscoda County?
faqs.answer: Send us your deed or probate documentation along with any royalty statements you have. We'll check current activity and production tied to your specific section and give you a straight answer on what it's realistically worth.
